# k100

Run the Corsair K100 RGB keyboard without iCUE, on Windows and Linux.

[![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-blue)](#license)

## Installation

Building needs Rust 1.95 or newer. On Linux install `pkg-config` first.

```sh
cargo build --release -p daemon -p k100-cli
```

This produces `k100d` (the daemon that owns the keyboard) and `k100` (the command line and the GUI) in `target/release/`. Keep both in the same folder: `k100 daemon` and `k100 gui` look for `k100d` next to themselves.

### Windows

1. Close iCUE. The daemon will not take the keyboard while iCUE, ckb-next, OpenRGB, OpenLinkHub or SignalRGB is running. If one of them is running but does not control the K100, list its process name under `ignore_conflicts` in `settings.toml`.
2. Put `k100.exe` and `k100d.exe` in one folder, then run `k100 daemon` and `k100 gui`.
3. To start the daemon at every login run `k100 autostart on`. `k100 autostart off` removes it again.

The tray icon is part of `k100d`. Its menu switches profiles, opens the GUI, releases the keyboard to its own lighting and quits the daemon. Double-clicking the icon opens the GUI.

### Linux

1. Let your user open the keyboard and create virtual input devices:

   ```sh
   sudo install -m 644 packaging/linux/70-k100.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/
   echo uinput | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k100.conf
   sudo modprobe uinput
   sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger
   ```

   Then unplug and replug the keyboard.
2. Install the binaries and the application menu entry:

   ```sh
   sudo install -m 755 target/release/k100d target/release/k100 /usr/local/bin/
   install -Dm 644 packaging/linux/k100.desktop ~/.local/share/applications/k100.desktop
   ```

3. Run `k100 daemon`, then `k100 gui`.
4. To start the daemon at login, run `k100 autostart on` (it writes an XDG autostart entry), or use the systemd user unit instead:

   ```sh
   install -Dm 644 packaging/linux/k100d.service ~/.config/systemd/user/k100d.service
   systemctl --user enable --now k100d
   ```

   Enable only one of `k100 autostart on` and the systemd unit, and run `k100 autostart off` before you enable the unit.

The tray icon needs GTK 3 and libayatana-appindicator, so it is only built when you ask for it. Install `libgtk-3-dev` and `libayatana-appindicator3-dev`, then build the daemon with `cargo build --release -p daemon --features tray`. Without that feature `k100d` runs with no tray icon.

Audio capture for the audio visualizer needs a PulseAudio server or PipeWire with pipewire-pulse; check with `k100 diag audio`.

## Usage

`k100d` runs in the background and is the only program that talks to the keyboard. `k100 gui`, the tray and the command line all talk to it over a local socket, so you can use any of them together.

`k100 gui` shows the keyboard and has panes for lighting layers, key assignments and macros (select a key and record a macro into it, then click Stop), the dial modes, device settings, profiles and onboard profiles. If the daemon is not running, the window offers to start it.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `k100 status` | Show the keyboard, active profile, brightness, polling rate, WinLock, dial mode and autostart |
| `k100 profile list`, `set <name>`, `show <name>`, `import <file>`, `export <name> <file>` | Manage profiles |
| `k100 brightness <0-100>` | Set the brightness |
| `k100 polling <hz>` | Set the USB polling rate (125 to 8000) |
| `k100 effect <name> [--color #rrggbb]` | Put an effect on top of the active profile; `k100 effect off` removes it |
| `k100 winlock <on\|off>` | Turn WinLock on or off |
| `k100 release`, `k100 reacquire` | Hand the keyboard back to its own lighting, or take it again |
| `k100 daemon [--foreground] [-- <k100d options>]` | Start the daemon in the background, or run it in the foreground |
| `k100 autostart <on\|off\|status>` | Start the daemon at login |
| `k100 keys` | List the key names you can use in profiles |
| `k100 events` | Print key, dial and state events |
| `k100 onboard list` | List the profiles stored on the keyboard |
| `k100 onboard save <profile> [--slot N] [--dry-run]` | Save a profile to the keyboard, as a new slot or over slot N. `--dry-run` shows what would be written without touching the keyboard |
| `k100 onboard delete <slot>`, `k100 onboard activate <slot>` | Remove a stored profile, or choose the one the keyboard plays |
| `k100 onboard backup [--to DIR]`, `k100 onboard restore <folder>` | Copy every stored profile to a folder, or put them back from one |
| `k100 sdk block <exe>`, `k100 sdk unblock <exe>` | Refuse an iCUE SDK app by its exe name, or allow it again |
| `k100 diag <subcommand>` | Low-level hardware checks (stop the daemon first, except for `diag audio`) |
| `k100 diag audio [--seconds N]` | Print the captured audio spectrum as text, with no keyboard or daemon needed |
| `k100 diag file <id> [--out PATH]` | Read one file from the keyboard's onboard memory (for example `0x0f`, the stored profile list) and print it as hex |
| `k100 diag file-write <id> <path> [--create]`, `k100 diag file-remove <id>` | Replace or remove an onboard file (create and remove only for free-use ids 0x6D60..0x7FFF). These change the keyboard's stored profiles |
| `k100 diag prop <id> [--set N]` | Read a device property by id, optionally writing it first |
| `k100 diag sdk-probe [--write] [--out FILE]` | Talk to whatever serves the iCUE SDK pipe and save every message as JSON. Without `--write` it only reads |
| `k100 diag sdk-compare <expected> <actual>` | Compare two probe transcripts and list the differences |

The effects are `solid`, `rainbow_wave`, `spiral_rainbow`, `color_wave`, `visor`, `color_pulse`, `rain`, `type`, `ripple` and `audio_visualizer`. All but the rainbow ones and `audio_visualizer` need `--color`. The audio visualizer shows the system audio output as 32 frequency bands across the keyboard, and `--color` gives it a single color instead of its green to red gradient.

`k100d` takes `--config-dir <path>` to use a different configuration folder and `--no-tray` to skip the tray icon. Pass them through `k100`, for example `k100 daemon -- --config-dir ./config`.

### Files

Settings and profiles are plain TOML. They live in `%APPDATA%\k100\config\` on Windows and in `~/.config/k100/` on Linux. `settings.toml` holds the keyboard settings and `profiles/<name>.toml` holds one profile each. The daemon applies a change when you save a file, and keeps the last working version of a file that has an error. This profile shows layers, key actions, macros and dial modes:

```toml
name = "actions"

[[layers]]
name = "base"
zone = "all"
effect = { type = "solid", color = "#102030" }

[[layers]]
name = "alert"
zone = "keys"
enabled = false
effect = { type = "solid", color = "#ff0000" }

[[assignments]]
key = "g1"
action = { type = "text", text = "Hello from the K100" }

[[assignments]]
key = "g2"
action = { type = "macro", steps = [{ down = "left_ctrl" }, { tap = "c" }, { up = "left_ctrl" }] }

[[assignments]]
key = "g3"
action = { type = "lighting_trigger", layer = "alert", duration_ms = 1500 }

[[assignments]]
key = "g4"
action = { type = "open_url", url = "https://github.com/Garulf/corsair-keyboard" }

[[assignments]]
key = "g5"
action = { type = "mouse", button = "middle" }

[[assignments]]
key = "caps_lock"
action = { type = "remap", key = "escape" }
pass_through = ["shift"]

[[dial.modes]]
kind = "brightness"

[[dial.modes]]
kind = "macro_recording"

[[dial.modes]]
kind = "track_selector"

[[dial.modes]]
kind = "vertical_scroll"
```

### Onboard profiles

Lighting layers, key actions and macros live in the profile files on your computer, and k100d plays them while it controls the keyboard. `k100 onboard save <profile>` also copies a profile into the keyboard's own memory as a new slot, or over an existing one with `--slot N`. A saved slot plays when the keyboard is in hardware mode, which is when k100d is not running or has released the keyboard (`k100 release`). `k100 onboard activate <slot>` chooses which stored slot plays, and `k100 onboard list` shows the slots, the active one and the free space.

The keyboard stores less than a profile file can describe. Layers become hardware effects, key actions and macros become stored assignments, and the dial modes that have a hardware equivalent are kept. Whatever the keyboard cannot hold is left out or approximated, and `save` prints one line for each. `k100 onboard save <profile> --dry-run` prints the same report, plus the files it would write, without touching the keyboard. A slot holds at most 20 lighting effects, so lower layers are dropped past that. Deleting the only slot is refused.

While k100d runs, the onboard commands go through it, and the keyboard shows a change once k100d releases the keyboard or quits. Without k100d, `k100` opens the keyboard itself, and it refuses to if k100d is running but does not answer. After a change made that way the keyboard is switched back to hardware mode, so it shows the result at once. `--config-dir` picks the config folder for that direct access and for dry runs.

Before every save, delete and restore, the keyboard's slots are copied to a new folder under `onboard-backup/` in the config folder, and the command prints its path. `k100 onboard restore <folder>` puts all slots in that folder back, and `k100 onboard backup [--to DIR]` makes a copy on demand.

The GUI's Onboard pane does the same through k100d: it lists the stored slots with the active one marked, saves the edited profile as a new slot or over the selected one after a preview of what is left out, activates and deletes slots, and backs them up and restores them. Saving uses the profile as it was last applied, so apply your edits first. Restore takes the full path of a backup folder, and "Use the latest backup" fills in the folder of the last backup k100d reported. While k100d has released the keyboard the pane offers to take it back first.

### iCUE SDK apps (Windows)

With iCUE closed, apps that use version 4 of the iCUE SDK talk to k100d instead. Elgato Stream Deck's Corsair G-key support and the SDK lighting in some games are the usual ones. k100d is compatible with the iCUE SDK and is not iCUE. It accepts at most 32 SDK connections at once and drops further ones.

- Stream Deck only connects while a program named `iCUE.exe` is running, so while the SDK is enabled k100d runs a copy of itself under that name from the `icue-standin` folder in the config folder. The copy does nothing and exits with k100d. Stream Deck looks for it when it starts, so start k100d first, or restart Stream Deck once after k100d starts. k100d does not count its own copy as a running iCUE.
- An app that asks for exclusive G-key control takes the G-keys it intercepts, and their k100d actions pause until it lets go or disconnects.
- Each app's lighting sits above your profile, unless the app asks for a priority of 127 or lower, which puts it underneath. An app that asks for exclusive lighting replaces the profile's lighting while it holds it.
- `k100 status` and the GUI's Overview list the connected apps and what each one holds. The Overview has Block and Unblock buttons, and `k100 sdk block <exe>` does the same from the command line. Blocking an app that is connected disconnects it.
- If iCUE was running when k100d started, it owns the SDK pipe. k100d waits, tries again every 10 s, and shows "in use by another program". Start iCUE only while k100d is stopped, since both would also fight over the keyboard.
- Older games on the v3 SDK or Corsair's Game SDK are not supported yet.

The `[sdk]` table in `settings.toml` has these keys:

- `enabled` (default `true`): with `enabled = false` k100d does not offer the SDK, so a running iCUE can serve SDK apps.
- `exclusive_control` (default `true`): with `false`, requests for exclusive lighting or G-key control are refused and apps run shared.
- `blocked` (default empty): exe names to refuse. `k100 sdk block` edits this list.
- `device_id`: the id k100d reports for the keyboard. It is generated once and saved. To keep Stream Deck's existing G-key bindings, set it to the id iCUE reported for the keyboard: run `k100 diag sdk-probe` while iCUE is running and k100d is stopped, and copy the K100's `id` from the transcript. k100d picks up the change without a restart.
- `trace` (default `false`): write every SDK message to `logs/sdk-trace.jsonl` in the config folder. Tracing stops at 16 MiB with a notice as the last line. Restart k100d, or switch `trace` off and on, to start a fresh file; the full one is kept as `sdk-trace.old.jsonl`.

### Things to know

- The keyboard stays in software mode while the daemon runs and goes back to its own lighting when the daemon stops cleanly. After a hard kill run `k100 diag release`.
- Per-program profile switching follows the foreground window and works on Windows only.
- Key actions are sent with `SendInput` on Windows and through a `uinput` device on Linux. On Windows, programs that ignore injected input (some games) and windows running as administrator do not see them.
- The key debounce value in the Device pane is in firmware units, from 0 to 300. The keyboard's own default is 30, and the unit is not known to be milliseconds.
- The GUI draws the ANSI layout. On other layouts the labels in the picture may not match the physical keys.
